summary.text: Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other.
If one event does change the likelihood of another, the events are dependent.
For more than two events, mutual independence is stronger than pairwise independence: mutual implies pairwise, but not the other way around.

facts.label: Dice example
facts.value: A 6 on the first roll and a 6 on the second are independent

facts.label: A dependent pair
facts.value: A 6 first and a sum of 8 are not independent

facts.label: Cards with replacement
facts.value: Red on the first draw and red on the second are independent

facts.label: Zero covariance
facts.value: Two random variables can have covariance 0 and still be dependent

facts.label: Default meaning
facts.value: Plain independence usually means mutual independence

items.prompt: You roll a die twice. Event A is a 6 on the first roll and event B is a 6 on the second. How are they related?

options.label: Independent, since the first roll does not affect the second
Dependent, since a 6 makes another 6 more likely
Dependent, since a 6 makes another 6 less likely
Neither, since the rolls happen at different times

items.explain: The occurrence of a 6 on the first roll does not change the probability of a 6 on the second, so the events are independent.

items.prompt: You roll a die twice. Event A is a 6 on the first roll and event C is that the two rolls add up to 8. How are they related?

options.label: Independent, since each roll is separate from the other
Independent, since the total is a different kind of event
Dependent, since the roll tells you nothing about the total
Dependent, since the first roll affects how likely that total is

items.explain: A 6 on the first roll and a sum of 8 are not independent: one occurring changes the likelihood of the other.

items.prompt: From a deck, you draw a card, note its colour, put it back, shuffle, and draw again. Event A is red on the first draw and B is red on the second. How are they related?

options.label: Dependent, since the first card was red
Independent, since putting the card back resets the deck
Dependent, since the same deck is used twice
Neither, since the draws are unrelated to colour

items.explain: With the card replaced, a red first card and a red second card are independent events.

items.prompt: Three events are set up so that every pair among them is independent. Can you be sure all three are mutually independent?

options.label: Yes, since mutual independence just means every pair is independent
Yes, since a third event cannot undo what holds for pairs
No, since pairwise independence does not guarantee mutual independence
No, since three events can never be independent at all

items.explain: Mutual independence implies pairwise independence, but not the other way around.

items.prompt: Two quantities are measured and their covariance turns out to be exactly zero. A friend says that proves they are independent. Is that right?

options.label: Yes, since zero covariance means one never affects the other
Yes, but only if the quantities are whole numbers
No, since both quantities would then have to be constant
No, since quantities with zero covariance can still be dependent

items.explain: Independence is not implied by a covariance of 0: such variables may still be dependent.

items.prompt: A shop notices that whenever the weather forecast says rain, umbrella sales jump. What does this say about forecast rain and umbrella sales?

options.label: They are dependent, since one changes the likelihood of the other
They are independent, since they are different kinds of event
They are independent, since sales happen only after the forecast
They are mutually independent, since there are two events

items.explain: Dependence is when the occurrence of one event does affect the likelihood of another.
